newsitem.title: USA: Sterling slides sharply on remarks from Britain's Clarke.
newsitem.headline: Sterling slides sharply on remarks from Britain's Clarke.

text.p: The British pound fell sharply against other major currencies Tuesday after a top British government official expressed concern about sterling's recent strength.

The pound slid against the mark, the yen and the dollar, falling to a one-month low against the U.S. unit before ending the session at $1.6445, over three-and-a-half cents lower than its close Monday at $1.6802.

"Sterling was absolutely crushed," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co. "The last few weeks everybody has been buying sterling and selling almost everything else and all that was reversed with the most obvious impact on the yen."
The impetus for the pound's decline came from British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, who said British business was starting to fret about sterling's rise.
"At the moment our currency is strengthening very strongly and large numbers of British industries are beginning to get worried that we might get too strong," Clarke told Parliament.

He also confirmed that Britain will be exempted from a proposed European stability pact in the run-up to a single currency. The remarks added to the pound's woes because they meant that Britain will not be bound to the same strict fiscal discipline as other countries seeking to join European Economic and Monetary Union in 1999.

Further aggravating weakness in the pound were remarks from Bank of England Governor Eddie George, who said he was not surprised by sterling's downward correction. Talk that the British central bank was actively selling sterling to stem its recent rise also weighed on the currency.
In other trading, the dollar was mixed, climbing modestly to 1.5565 marks from 1.5555 at Monday's close, but sliding substantially against the yen to 113.27 from 114.53.

Traders said the yen's strong performance against the pound contributed to weakness in the dollar/yen rate. They said a hesitancy to purchase dollars against yen at heady levels also contributed to the dollar's decline.
"People are afraid to be buyers up to the 115 level," said Strauss.
Strength against the mark was fuelled by overnight comments from New York Federal Reserve President William McDonough and weak German industrial production numbers, traders said.
McDonough, speaking in Hong Kong, predicted the dollar would gain in status as European Economic and Monetary Union nears.
Meanwhile, German industrial production fell 1.8 percent in October after forecasters had predicted a modest rise. The weaker-than-expected numbers fuelled talk of a German interest rate cut.
"The McDonough statements and industrial production numbers from Germany were the main reason why the dollar rallied overnight," said Brian McCarthy, market analyst at Ruesch International.
Elsewhere, speculation about an Australian interest rate cut took the dollar sharply higher against the Australian dollar. The Australian dollar ended around $0.7980, down from $0.8165.
The dollar closed slightly lower at 1.3206 Swiss francs versus 1.3215 at Monday's close. The dollar also fell modestly to Canadian $1.3500 against C$1.3513.
